column1: # The file service's traces: what a host's end of xpute's system calls owes a guest (ipc/sys,
# ARCHITECTURE.md's system calls), apart from the boundary's rules C0 to C7 — the boundary
# carries the calls, and this is what they mean. Run against the host's end
# (ts/host/src/ipc/sys.test.ts): a step writes a record as a guest's turn would, `turn`
# runs them as the host does after a turn, and what reaches the guest is held to the trace.
#   file R P B        the host's file P below root R: its bytes in hex, ENOENT, or `later` —
#                     answered only when a `deliver` says, as a transport answers
#   openat FD R F P   a guest's OPENAT: FD as the guest issued it (slot and generation), F rd or wr,
#                     P the path, `""` for an empty one
#   read FD N / write FD TEXT / close FD
#   turn              the host runs the turn's records
#   deliver R P B     the transport answers what `later` held, with B as `file` takes it
#   expect opened FD RES   the next answer the guest is sent: a size, or an errno by name
#   expect quiet      no answer the guest has not been held to
#   expect read HEX   what the last read put in the guest's memory
#   expect commit R P TEXT   what a close made the file
# An open's answer comes on a later turn, however much later: `later` is how a trace says the
# transport is slow, and nothing here fixes how many turns pass.

column2: open.later open.absent read write close.opening stale.reuse root.walk

column1: # Opened to write and closed in one turn: the close commits what was written, and the open, ended
# before it was answered, is answered nothing.
# A close ends a descriptor still opening: its open is never answered, however late its transport.
# The slot a closed descriptor held is issued again under a new generation before the old open's
# transport answers: the late answer reaches neither descriptor, and the new one gets its own.
# A root is the whole of what it grants: a path walks down from it a name at a time, and a name
# that is empty, `.` or `..` — an absolute path's first among them — is refused before any host sees it.
